sentences.cn_text: 作为一名历史学家，我始终在寻找能够让我们重新审视过去的文本或图像，我已经开始专注于寻找那些展示维多利亚时代祖先微笑的照片（还有什么比这更能打破19世纪拘谨形象呢？）。
sentences.en_text: As a historian who’s always searching for the text or the image that makes us reevaluate the past, I’ve become preoccupied with looking for photographs that show our Victorian ancestors smiling (what better way to shatter the image of 19th-century prudery?).

sentences.cn_text: 我找到了不少这样的照片，并且自从我开始在推特上发布它们以来，它们引起了相当大的轰动。
sentences.en_text: I’ve found quite a few, and — since I started posting them on Twitter — they have been causing quite a stir.

sentences.cn_text: 人们惊讶地看到有证据表明维多利亚时代的人有乐趣，并且能够笑，也确实会笑。
sentences.en_text: People have been surprised to see evidence that Victorians had fun and could, and did, laugh.

sentences.cn_text: 他们注意到，随着将我们分隔开来的百年光阴通过共同的笑声体验而逐渐消逝，维多利亚时代的人似乎突然变得更加人性化了。
sentences.en_text: They are noting that the Victorians suddenly seem to become more human as the hundred-or-so years that separate us fade away through our common experience of laughter.

sentences.cn_text: 当然，我需要承认，我收藏的「微笑的维多利亚人」照片仅占1840年至1900年间创作的大量摄影肖像中的极小一部分，其中大多数展示的是被摄者在画布背景前痛苦而僵硬地摆姿势，或者茫然地凝视着中距处。
sentences.en_text: Of course, I need to concede that my collection of “Smiling Victorians” makes up only a tiny percentage of the vast catalogue of photographic portraiture created between 1840 and 1900, the majority of which show sitters posing miserably and stiffly in front of painted backdrops, or staring absently into the middle distance.

sentences.cn_text: 我们如何解释这一现象？
sentences.en_text: How do we explain this trend?

sentences.cn_text: 在19世纪40年代和50年代摄影的早期阶段，曝光时间以极其漫长而著称：银版摄影法（在镀银铜板上生成图像）可能需要几分钟才能完成，导致被摄者移动位置或调整肢体时图像变得模糊。
sentences.en_text: During the 1840s and 1850s, in the early days of photography, exposure times were notoriously long: the daguerreotype photographic method (producing an image on a silvered copper plate) could take several minutes to complete, resulting in blurred images as sitters shifted position or adjusted their limbs.

sentences.cn_text: 想到在相机执行其神奇职责时要保持固定的笑容实在太难以想象，因此一种不置可否的茫然凝视成为了常态。
sentences.en_text: The thought of holding a fixed grin as the camera performed its magical duties was too much to contemplate, and so a noncommittal blank stare became the norm.

sentences.cn_text: 但到了19世纪80年代，曝光时间已经快得多了，而Box Brownie及其他便携式相机的引入意味着，虽然按今天的数字标准仍显缓慢，但曝光几乎是瞬间完成的。
sentences.en_text: But exposure times were much quicker by the 1880s, and the introduction of the Box Brownie and other portable cameras meant that, though slow by today’s digital standards, the exposure was almost instantaneous.

sentences.cn_text: 到了19世纪90年代，捕捉自然的微笑相对容易了，因此我们必须从其他方面寻找维多利亚人仍然不愿微笑的原因。
sentences.en_text: Spontaneous smiles were relatively easy to capture by the 1890s, so we must look elsewhere for an explanation of why Victorians still hesitated to smile.

sentences.cn_text: 一个解释可能是通过夸张的笑容所表现出的尊严丧失。
sentences.en_text: One explanation might be the loss of dignity displayed through a cheesy grin.

sentences.cn_text: 「自然赋予我们嘴唇来遮盖牙齿」，一条流行的维多利亚时代谚语如此说道，暗指在专业牙科诞生之前，口腔的卫生状况往往令人震惊。
sentences.en_text: “Nature gave us lips to conceal our teeth,” ran one popular Victorian saying, alluding to the fact that before the birth of proper dentistry, mouths were often in a shocking state of hygiene.

sentences.cn_text: 一口健康洁白、整齐的「珍珠白」牙齿在维多利亚社会中是罕见的景象，是超级富豪的专属（即便如此，牙齿卫生也无法得到保证）。
sentences.en_text: A flashing set of healthy and clean, regular “pearly whites” was a rare sight in Victorian society, the preserve of the super-rich (and even then, dental hygiene was not guaranteed).

sentences.cn_text: 露齿的笑容（尤其是当牙齿有缺口或变黑时）缺乏品位：醉汉、流浪汉和音乐厅表演者可能会像刘易斯·卡罗尔笔下露牙龈的柴郡猫那样龇牙咧嘴地笑，但这对于受过良好教养的人来说并不是一种得体的表情。
sentences.en_text: A toothy grin (especially when there were gaps or blackened teeth) lacked class: drunks, tramps, and music hall performers might gurn and grin with a smile as wide as Lewis Carroll’s gum-exposing Cheshire Cat, but it was not a becoming look for properly bred persons.

sentences.cn_text: 即使是喜欢开怀大笑的马克·吐温也说过，在摄影肖像方面，「没有什么比一个愚蠢、傻气的笑容永远定格更具破坏性的了」。
sentences.en_text: Even Mark Twain, a man who enjoyed a hearty laugh, said that when it came to photographic portraits there could be “nothing more damning than a silly, foolish smile fixed forever”.
